caption:
Turn your phone grey tonight. A boring phone is easier to put down.

WHY: bright app icons and red badges are built to catch your eye. With colour off, the same apps just look less tempting.

THE STUDY: 84 young adults (average age 22) let an app log their phone use for 2 weeks. Week 1 normal, week 2 in grayscale. In the grey week they spent about 20 minutes less a day on their phones, and said they felt more in control of their phone use and less stressed.

HOW:
1. iPhone: Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Color Filters. Turn it on and pick Grayscale.
2. Android: open Settings and search "grayscale" (on many phones it's under Accessibility > Color correction).
3. Optional: add it to your Accessibility Shortcut so you can switch colour back for photos and maps.
4. Keep it on for one full week before you judge it.

THE CATCH: they picked up their phones just as often (about 80 times a day both weeks). The visits got shorter, not fewer. It was one week and 84 people, and it didn't change their sleep or how productive they felt.

Do this: turn on Grayscale tonight.

Send this to the friend who says "one quick scroll" and loses an hour.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

#focus #screentime #digitalwellbeing #productivity #phonehabits
first_comment: Source: Dekker, C. A., & Baumgartner, S. E. (2024). Is life brighter when your phone is not? The efficacy of a grayscale smartphone intervention addressing digital well-being. Mobile Media & Communication, 12(3). https://doi.org/10.1177/20501579231212062 (open access, first online Nov 9 2023). 84 young adults (Android users, mean age 21.95, recruited through a university lab pool and the first author's network), 1 baseline week then 1 grayscale week, phone use logged by an app: daily screen time 287 -> 268 min (about 20 min less a day); daily unlocks did not change (80.03 vs 80.33, p = .86); perceived overuse, online vigilance and stress went down; no effect on productivity or sleep. Settings paths checked Oct 25 2026 on Apple Support (support.apple.com/en-us/111773: Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Color Filters, Grayscale) and Google Android Accessibility Help (support.google.com/accessibility/android/answer/11183305: Accessibility > Color and motion > Color correction; menus vary by phone).

caption:
For whoever studies on their phone: you understand more on paper.

WHY: researchers think screens nudge us to skim, and we feel more sure we got it than we really did. On paper, people tend to read more slowly and carefully.

THE RESEARCH: a review of 54 studies with 171,055 readers found people understood texts better on paper than on screens. The gap was biggest when people were reading against the clock and reading to learn (textbooks, articles, work documents). For stories and novels there was no real difference. And the paper advantage got bigger in newer studies, not smaller.

HOW:
1. Pick the pages you'll be tested on, or the document you must really understand.
2. Print them (a library or campus printer works).
3. Read with a pen in hand. Mark the 2 or 3 lines that matter.
4. Keep the screen for quick lookups and reading for fun.

THE CATCH: the paper advantage is small on average, and it's about understanding, not speed. If printing isn't possible, slow down on screen and avoid scrolling while you read.

Do this: print the pages you must understand.

Send this to whoever studies on their phone.

Follow for one small focus fix a day, each one backed by research.

#studytips #studying #focus #reading #studentlife
first_comment: Source: Delgado, P., Vargas, C., Ackerman, R., & Salmerón, L. (2018). Don't throw away your printed books: A meta-analysis on the effects of reading media on reading comprehension. Educational Research Review, 25, 23–38. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2018.09.003 54 studies, 171,055 participants: comprehension was better on paper than on screen (g = −0.21). The advantage was larger under time limits than self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative-only texts, and grew from 2000 to 2017. Checked against the authors' PDF (uv.es) and the University of Haifa record, Oct 25 2026.
